title: 6yo M - Severe Asthma Exacerbation
background: Parents bring their 6-year-old son to the ER during high PM 2.5 season. He has a known history of asthma. He has been using his Salbutamol inhaler at home with no relief.

exam.finding: Restless, sitting up, using accessory muscles (suprasternal retractions), speaking in single words.
Decreased breath sounds bilaterally, prolonged expiratory phase, loud inspiratory and expiratory wheezing.

investigations.name: Chest X-Ray
investigations.report: Hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm. No consolidation or pneumothorax.

start.narrative: A child presents with a severe asthma exacerbation (SpO2 88%, retractions, speaking in single words). Immediate action is required.

correct_o2_neb.narrative: SpO2 improves to 94% with Oxygen. Nebulized bronchodilators help open the airways, but the wheezing and retractions persist. What is the next critical step?

wrong_intubate.narrative: Intubating a severe asthmatic is high risk (bronchospasm, barotrauma) and should be an absolute last resort. You should have maximized medical therapy first. The child rapidly desaturates.

wrong_sedate.narrative: Sedating an asthmatic patient suppresses their respiratory drive. The child stops breathing adequately and goes into respiratory arrest!

wrong_discharge.narrative: This is a severe, life-threatening exacerbation! Discharging this child without acute treatment and observation is medical negligence.

correct_steroids.narrative: Excellent. Systemic corticosteroids reduce the underlying airway inflammation. After 1 hour, the retractions resolve, wheezing decreases, and the child can speak in full sentences. Admit to pediatric ward.

magnesium_early.narrative: IV Magnesium Sulfate is a great adjunct for severe asthma, but steroids are the cornerstone of treating the inflammation and preventing relapse. You must give steroids.
